title: Part 1 - Why most financial institutions are getting 'AI for customer experience' wrong
snippet: Financial institutions are on the verge of repeating the same mistake they made with telephone banking, internet banking and mobile banking: treating AI as another standalone service layer. In the first of...
fullText:
Financial institutions are on the verge of repeating the same mistake they made with telephone banking, internet banking and mobile banking: treating AI as another standalone service layer. In the first of our six-part series, we look at why the next phase of transformation will mean orchestrating end-to-end experiences, where AI works across the entire customer journey, carrying context across digital, conversational and human touchpoints. 
          

      

When financial institutions introduced telephone banking, internet banking and mobile banking, each new channel improved access. However, very few institutions truly redesigned the end-to-end experience around the customer. Instead, they created parallel service models, fragmented ownership and disconnected journeys. 

AI is now arriving in much the same way: layered in as another interface, another team, and another capability layer.

The pattern is easy to recognize. Smarter chatbots. Advanced Intelligent Virtual Agents (IVAs), powered by voice AI. More capable copilots. Increasing use of natural language and automation. Too often, these capabilities are being bolted onto already-broken journeys, rather than used to fundamentally redesign the customer experience.

What makes this transition different is the speed. AI is being adopted faster than any technology before. Generative AI has outpaced the uptake of both the PC and the internet, with tools like ChatGPT reaching mass adoption in months, not years.1

However, when AI is applied by financial institutions to fragmented customer journeys, the frictions increase. Customers moving from ‘app’ to ‘chat’ to ‘voice’ find they must repeat information to solve an issue. Service agents gain another tool, but not the customer context that would make it meaningful. Costs and frictions shift between channels rather than disappearing.

The fundamental issue is that the financial industry has a channel-era design problem. AI is just scaling it.

Capco and Raconteur research found that 62% of financial services leaders are planning major customer journey redesigns within 12 months, rising to 90% within five years.2 At the same time, the Bank of England and FCA’s 2024 survey found that 75% of firms were already using AI, with another 10% planning to do so within three years.3 The market is moving quickly, however, the faster deployment of a flawed design model simply scales the flaws.

This is why the next phase of transformation must be about designing AI-Orchestrated Experiences, where AI works across the entire journey, carrying context across digital, conversational and human touchpoints. The value will come from designing unified, end-to-end journeys. 

Prioritize unified journeys, not channels and chatbots

The customer experience is driven by their overall journey, not individual channels. However, most organizations still behave as though channels are the unit of design.

Digital teams optimize task completion in the app or on the website. Contact centers optimize handling time and containment rates, i.e. the ability to resolve issues inside their channel. Chat teams optimize deflection, i.e. diverting customers to self-service rather than human-assisted channels. Operations teams optimize the throughput of each process. 

Each function improves its own metrics, but the customer pays the price of the gaps and frictions in between. These are becoming harder to ignore. 

Capco’s recent work on conversational banking makes the point clearly: while financial services may have achieved multi-channel choice, omnichannel is the true end-state. Customers expect to start in one channel, continue in another and reach resolution without losing context. Isolated chatbot or IVA teams risk exacerbating fragmentation rather than reducing it.

This matters because AI deployed at the channel level inherits the channel’s limitations. A chatbot embedded on a website can only see what sits in front of it. A voice bot optimized for call deflection is incentivized to contain rather than resolve the customer issue. An agent copilot layered onto a customer service agent’s fragmented desktop can generate suggestions, but may not increase clarity. 

Each tool may be more intelligent than its predecessor. But disconnected from journey context, it just becomes a faster way of reproducing friction.

That is why so many institutions are seeing a familiar pattern. More AI is being deployed but the overall customer experience is not getting better.

Smarter chatbots and IVAs will still fail if the journey is broken

It would be easy to look at the last decade and conclude that conversational AI does not work in financial services. The story is more specific. Chat failed not because customers dislike a chat channel but because it was implemented in isolation from the journeys it was meant to support.

This is most visible in three journey types where fragmentation carries a high cost: servicing, fraud and claims.

    

In servicing, customers usually want speed, low effort and continuity. AI that cannot recognize what the customer has already tried, carry context into assisted service, or guide them through an exception without starting over just shifts the failure to a different moment in the journey.

    

In fraud, the stakes are higher. Customers may be anxious, vulnerable or under time pressure. They need an orchestrated response that recognizes urgency, gathers relevant context, prioritizes risk, and moves smoothly into human support whenever judgement is required.

    

In claims, the failure of standalone AI can become even more obvious. Imagine a claims build with a UK insurer, where the team spend weeks designing the ‘first notification of loss’ conversation – only to discover at testing that the AI cannot see what the customer had submitted online the day before. With the customer effectively being asked to start over, the team would need to rebuild the journey to carry context across before launch.

Claims, in particular, are rarely one interaction. They are a series of moments: notification, data capture, status updates, clarification, exceptions, settlement and, sometimes, complaint. A disconnected bot may help with one of those moments, but only embedding AI into the wider journey can transform the experience.

Other evidence from the UK points in the same direction. Research by the Digital Regulation Cooperation Forum (DRCF) found that consumers see GenAI as one stage in a broader process rather than a complete solution, and still want the option to speak with specialists, especially for bigger financial decisions or where financial resilience is lower.4 That should change how firms design AI, not how fast they adopt it.

The real opportunity is AI-Orchestrated Experiences

Value from AI will come from rethinking the experience end to end, not from deploying the most tools. At Capco, we call that AI-Orchestrated Experiences, i.e. treating AI as the orchestration layer across the customer journey, not as another channel feature. 

AI should understand intent, retain context, support decisioning, and guide the next best action. It should personalize and contextualize the experience in real time, without losing control, transparency or trust. AI should be embedded across products and journeys, rather than deployed through fragmented pilots.

This is also where UK market context matters. The FCA has been clear that existing frameworks apply to AI including Consumer Duty, accountability and governance. In practice, that raises the bar for customer journey design. If AI creates unreasonable barriers, breaks continuity or removes appropriate human support, the problem becomes a governance failure, not just a design one.

This is why the winners in the next phase will think differently. They will ask “where can AI reduce friction without removing trust?” rather than “where can we deploy AI?” They will design servicing journeys that prevent failure rather than merely absorbing demand. They will design fraud journeys that orchestrate urgency, reassurance and escalation. They will design claims journeys that connect moments in the overall customer experience, rather than digitizing them in isolation.

And they will recognize something that many institutions still have not fully accepted: human support becomes more important in an AI-enabled future, especially in the moments that matter most. Capco and Raconteur’s research found that 99% of leaders expect human advisers to remain integral to customer journeys, yet fewer than one in ten feel very confident in their ability to build long-term trust through AI, and only 5% feel very confident about aligning with regulatory expectations. The challenge is how to orchestrate both human professionals and AI properly.

Adoption is happening fast. Design is lagging. That is a mistake, and it is one that many institutions – having spent the last decade untangling telephone, internet and mobile fragmentation – cannot afford to repeat.  

Technology will keep changing. However, design choices made now will define the customer experience for the next decade – opening up opportunities for those that recognize and solve the underlying problem earlier this time.

title: Part 3 - Anatomy of an AI chat that earns trust
snippet: The AI chat will become the most frequent form of interaction that many customers have with their bank, insurer or wealth manager – and financial institutions are investing accordingly. But are these chats...
fullText:
The AI chat will become the most frequent form of interaction that many customers have with their bank, insurer or wealth manager – and financial institutions are investing accordingly. But are these chats being built to serve customers, or to deflect them? In the third of our six-part series, we explore what trust means in the AI chat context and set out six principles for creating AI chats that customers are drawn to, rather than quickly learning to avoid.
          

      

A UK insurer was testing a new AI chat ahead of launch. The team was confident the experience was ready. Customer testing said otherwise. The most common feedback was not about wrong answers. Customers told them they did not trust the responses they were getting.

When the insurer engaged us to look closer, the AI’s reasoning was sound. The answers were defensible. The problem was that customers could not see what the AI was doing or how it had arrived at any given response. The chat was a black box.

We redesigned the experience to do two things. Show the customer in real time what the AI was doing. Explain the reasoning behind each answer in plain English. 

Same AI. Same underlying logic. Different interface. At the next round of testing, customer trust scores rose sharply. That experience captures everything this article is about. 

Most AI chat interfaces in UK financial services look identical. A box. A blinking cursor. A polite greeting. Underneath, very different briefs.

Every UK bank, insurer and wealth manager is building one of these right now. The teams designing them are making choices that will define the customer experience for the next decade.

Some are built to genuinely help the customer. Some are built to keep the customer away from a human. The customer can usually tell within two exchanges.

The interface often reveals the brief. Key signals include whether and how the chat shows its workings, what it lets the customer do, and when it hands over to a person. These look like design choices but they send a strong message about the institutional intentions behind the provision of the AI chat. 

Even well-intentioned institutions can mistakenly send the wrong signals to customers, if they get their interface wrong. Six principles separate a chat that customers come back to, from one they learn to avoid:

1. Transparency: show the workings

A customer asking about a missing payment does not want a confident answer that turns out to be wrong. They want to see what the AI is actually doing. Is it searching their account, or guessing from training data? Most current chats do not tell them.

Good chat interfaces show this. Bad ones hide it.

The principle is the same one that applies to a good human adviser. You trust the answer more when you can see how it was reached. The customer does not need a technical explanation. They need to see that something real is happening behind the response.

2. Explainability: say why

The insurer experiment showed why explainability sits alongside transparency, not below it. Once customers could see what the AI was doing, the next thing they wanted to understand was the reasoning behind any given answer.

Take a typical interaction. A customer asks why their insurance renewal premium has gone up by £85. The AI gives them the new figure with a one-line reason: “increased due to changes in your risk profile.”

The customer’s next question, every time, is “which bit, and by how much?”

A good chat can walk through it. How much of the increase came from a single claim. How much from a postcode-level risk reassessment. How much from market conditions. How much from optional cover the customer added at last renewal. 

The customer might still feel the increase is too high. They will at least understand what they are being charged for.

A bad chat gives the headline and stops. The customer is left with a number they has not been explained and that, for example, they cannot defend to their partner. In financial services, that is where trust starts to wear thin.

This is the difference between a chat that feels like a conversation and one that feels like a wall.

3. User control: let people stop

Customers need to be able to interrupt the AI. Stop a long response. Cancel an action. Undo something that was just done.

This sounds obvious. It is missing from most chats currently in production.

The reason is that interruption is harder to engineer. It is easier to let the AI finish. Easier to commit the action immediately. Easier for the bank, worse for the customer.

If a customer cannot stop the AI mid-flow, they will hesitate before using it for anything that matters. And that defeats the point.

4. Consent and autonomy: respect the choice

Some customers want a personalized experience. Some find it intrusive. Most are somewhere in between, and their preference shifts depending on what they are trying to do.

The chat should reflect this, for example, by offering a clear opt-in to AI features. The ability to disable personalization without losing access to the service. Honest, plain-language information about how data is being used and what the customer can change.

5. Actionable outputs: close the loop

A common failure mode is the AI that gives a perfect answer and then leaves the customer to do all the work themselves.

“You can update your address through online banking.” Fine. But the customer is in the chat. Why are they being sent somewhere else?

How those actions happen also matters. Customers are comfortable giving instructions conversationally. They are less comfortable confirming consequential actions through chat alone.

A customer can tell the chat to send £200 to a friend without thinking twice. What they want before pressing send is a visual confirmation: a clear panel inside the chat showing the recipient, the amount, the date, the reference. A button to confirm. A button to cancel. The same pattern they already trust from their mobile banking app.

This is where multimodal design matters. The conversational layer takes the instruction. A visual layer, designed to feel like the existing mobile experience, confirms the action before it happens.

Good chat experiences combine both. They are a place where things actually happen, with the same level of trust the customer has in the rest of the bank’s digital experience.

6. Human oversight: know when to step back

The single most important question for any AI chat in financial services concerns when it should hand over the conversation to a skilled human professional.

Some interactions should never be fully automated. A vulnerable customer in distress. A complex claim. A regulated advice conversation. A complaint that has already escalated.

The chat needs to recognize these moments and route to a human, ideally without the customer having to ask. Confidence thresholds should trigger a human review. Sensitive topics should default to a human agent. The handover itself should be smooth: the human picks up where the AI left off, with full context, without making the customer repeat themselves.

Most banks are still treating the chat as the destination. The right design treats it as a layer, with a clear and well-rehearsed exit to a human.

The new front door

For most customers, the AI chat will become the most frequent interaction they have with their bank, insurer or wealth manager. More frequent than the app, the branch and the call center.

If they do not trust your AI chat, they do not trust you.

The technology to build the right kind of AI chat exists today. The constraint is the brief.

Which brings us back to the question that runs through this whole series. Are chats being built to serve customers, or to deflect them? The interface will tell you – and your customers – the answer.

title: Is Your Institution Ready for What’s Next? Five Questions for Middle East Financial Services Leaders
snippet: As Middle East banks move beyond experimentation, leaders face important decisions about where to invest, what to scale and how to deliver value. Capco's regional experts examine five questions shaping the future of banking, spanning cross-border payments, sovereign cloud, Agentic AI, tokenization and wealth management
fullText:
Banks across the Middle East are operating in an environment shaped by rapid technological advancement, shifting customer expectations, geopolitical developments and growing resilience requirements. Financial institutions are balancing innovation with regulatory priorities while looking for new ways to improve efficiency, unlock growth and remain competitive. With many technologies now moving beyond the pilot stage, the focus is increasingly shifting from experimentation to scalable implementation and measurable business outcomes.
          

      

Against this backdrop, we see five themes shaping the banking agenda through 2026 and into 2027: the rise of Agentic AI and AI-enabled operating models; the evolution of cross-border payments and settlement infrastructure; the growing momentum behind tokenization and digital assets; the transformation of wealth management through personalization and changing client expectations; and the increasing importance of sovereign cloud as organizations prioritize resilience, control, and AI readiness. Together, these trends offer a view of how the region’s banks are preparing for the next phase of industry evolution.

How are cross-border payments moving from messaging to intelligent settlement?

Cross-border payments have long been a critical part of the Middle East banking landscape. As one of the world's largest remittance corridors, the GCC processes billions of dollars in outbound payments each year, making payment efficiency a strategic priority for regional banks.

For decades, international payments have relied on correspondent banking networks and messaging infrastructure that can introduce delays, reconciliation complexity and significant liquidity requirements. Banks often need to maintain funds across multiple currencies and jurisdictions to support payment flows, tying up capital and increasing operational costs.

In 2026, that model is beginning to evolve.

Driven by advances in blockchain-enabled settlement and modernization initiatives from established payment networks such as SWIFT, banks are exploring new ways to improve the efficiency of cross-border transactions. Traditionally, SWIFT's role has been to facilitate secure messaging between financial institutions. However, the industry is increasingly looking beyond messaging towards optimizing settlement itself through greater transparency, payment finality and improved liquidity management.

One of the most significant developments is the emergence of solutions that enable banks to net obligations across payment flows, optimizing liquidity usage and reducing the capital tied up in cross-border payments. For GCC banks, where remittances represent a major business line, this could significantly reduce one of the largest cost components of cross-border payments.

At the same time, newer settlement models promise faster reconciliation, improved payment tracking and greater visibility across the transaction lifecycle. Unlike earlier blockchain initiatives, many of these solutions are designed to work alongside existing payment infrastructure and standards, lowering implementation barriers and accelerating adoption.

Importantly, the market is now moving beyond experimentation. Documentation for new blockchain-enabled settlement frameworks was released in 2026, with industry pilot testing scheduled throughout the summer and initial go-live activity expected later in the year. This signals a shift from proof-of-concept discussions to practical implementation.

As customer expectations for speed and transparency continue to rise, banks are increasingly focused on reducing friction across the entire payment lifecycle. In 2026, the future of cross-border payments will be defined by smarter settlement, optimized liquidity and greater visibility across global payment flows.

How is sovereign cloud shaping the future of digital residency to digital resilience?

For years, cloud adoption in the Middle East was primarily driven by scalability, efficiency and cost optimization. Today, the conversation is evolving. As governments, financial institutions, energy companies and other critical industries become increasingly dependent on digital services, cloud is no longer viewed simply as a technology platform; it is becoming a core part of the region’s digital infrastructure.

Recent regional disruptions have reinforced an important reality: cloud services are supported by physical infrastructure, including data centers, connectivity networks and power systems. For organizations operating in highly regulated and business-critical sectors, resilience is becoming just as important as performance. Leaders are increasingly asking not only where their data resides, but how their operations can continue during periods of disruption.

At the same time, hyperscalers are adapting to these changing requirements. AWS, Microsoft and Google Cloud continue to expand their regional presence while introducing new capabilities around data control, encryption, local partnerships and sovereignty-focused operating models. These developments are helping organizations meet regulatory requirements while strengthening operational control and resilience.

However, sovereign cloud is no longer simply about selecting a local cloud region. Organizations are increasingly adopting a sovereign-by-design approach, embedding resilience, governance, security and operational control into cloud strategies from the outset. This means understanding where critical workloads sit, reducing concentration risk, strengthening access controls and ensuring services can recover quickly when disruptions occur.

The rise of AI is adding further momentum to this shift. As organizations look to deploy AI at scale, they must ensure sensitive data, models and workloads remain protected and aligned with local requirements. In many ways, sovereign cloud is becoming the foundation for the next wave of AI adoption, providing the trust, security and control needed to unlock greater value from data and AI initiatives.

Looking ahead, cloud strategy in the Middle East will be defined by more than migration and modernization. Organizations will increasingly focus on building digital environments that balance innovation with resilience, helping them maintain continuity, protect critical assets and support future growth. As this trend continues to evolve, organizations will need to translate sovereignty requirements into practical decisions around architecture, risk, governance and operating models.

How is AI Agents taking on banking operations? Balancing automation, governance and oversight

Artificial intelligence is entering a new phase in financial services. After several years focused on GenAI tools that help employees search, summarize, analyze and generate content, attention is now turning to Agentic AI – systems capable of executing tasks and coordinating workflows while operating within defined controls and human oversight. For banks across the Middle East, this represents a significant shift.

Despite continued investment in digital transformation, many operational processes still rely heavily on human orchestration. Activities such as onboarding, KYC reviews, customer service, fraud monitoring and technology delivery often involve multiple handoffs, manual interventions and complex decision-making processes. Agentic AI offers an opportunity to streamline these activities by handling repetitive and structured tasks, allowing employees to focus on judgement-intensive work, customer interactions and exception management.

Rather than replacing people, the emerging model is one of collaboration, where AI agents perform specific activities while humans remain responsible for oversight, validation and decision-making. This is why many institutions begin with targeted use cases. Areas such as onboarding and KYC are particularly attractive because they rely on structured data, follow defined workflow and have clearly measurable outcomes.

Early experimentation is helping organizations understand where agentic systems can create value while also revealing the operational and governance requirements needed to support adoption at scale. As AI takes on a more active role in execution, governance is becoming a key differentiator. Institutions must look beyond traditional concerns such as data quality and model accuracy to address broader questions around accountability, auditability, control and the interaction between AI agents and human operators.

As a result, the conversation is increasingly shifting from technology to operating model design. The institutions that succeed will not necessarily be those deploying the most AI agents, but those that establish clear governance frameworks, define effective human-in-the-loop controls and build operating models that allow AI and people to work together safely and effectively.

Looking ahead, Agentic AI is likely to become a key enabler of productivity and scalability across banking operations. As organizations move from experimentation to adoption at scale, success will depend on establishing the right balance between automation, governance and human oversight.

How is tokenization moving from innovation to infrastructure?

The Middle East is rapidly establishing itself as a global hub for digital assets and tokenized finance. Supported by evolving regulatory frameworks, growing investment in financial market infrastructure and ambitious digital economy strategies, markets across the region are creating the foundations for tokenization to move beyond experimentation and into mainstream financial services.

The UAE has been at the forefront of this development, fostering regulated ecosystems where banks, exchanges, technology providers and regulators can collaborate to develop tokenized financial markets. Momentum is also broadening across the region. In Saudi Arabia, initiatives led by the Capital Market Authority (CMA) and Saudi Central Bank (SAMA) are supporting the modernization of capital markets, financial infrastructure and digital financial services. In Qatar, the Qatar Financial Centre (QFC) is helping develop the regulatory and institutional environment for digital assets, reinforcing the country’s wider ambitions around financial innovation and institutional capital.

Across these markets, institutions are expanding tokenized investment products, digital liquidity solutions and custody capabilities, while market infrastructure providers continue to strengthen the supporting ecosystem through advances in settlement, governance and shareholder servicing. Together, these developments are helping bridge the gap between distributed ledger technology and traditional financial markets, providing institutions with greater confidence to move from pilots toward scaled adoption.

For banks in the Middle East, the strategic question is no longer whether tokenization will become part of the financial landscape, but where to participate within the emerging ecosystem. Some institutions will focus on developing the infrastructure that supports tokenized markets, while others will prioritize client-facing services such as digital asset custody, tokenized investment products and wealth solutions. Many are likely to adopt hybrid approaches that combine infrastructure participation with new distribution and servicing capabilities.

Looking ahead, tokenization is expected to become an increasingly important component of the region's financial infrastructure. However, realizing its full potential will require more than adopting new technology. Banks will need interoperable platforms, robust governance, trusted digital custody and operating models that integrate tokenized assets seamlessly into existing banking and capital markets ecosystems.

How is wealth management shifting from product-led to relationship-led growth?

For decades, wealth management in the Middle East has been built on preserving and growing assets for high-net-worth clients. Today, that proposition is expanding. Rapid wealth creation, intergenerational wealth transfer and the emergence of regional financial hubs are reshaping client expectations, creating new opportunities for banks to deepen relationships while diversifying revenue beyond traditional banking services.

At the same time, the region is becoming an increasingly important destination for wealth itself. Financial centers such as Dubai and Abu Dhabi continue to strengthen their position as global wealth hubs, while Saudi Arabia’s significant concentration of high-net-worth and family office capital is being reinforced by regulatory reforms aimed at deepening its capital markets and investment ecosystem. Qatar adds another dimension, with its strong focus on sovereign capital deployment and a growing institutional family office landscape.

Together, these markets are attracting and retaining more capital through evolving regulation, sophisticated financial ecosystems and growing investor confidence. As more wealth remains within the region, banks have an opportunity to deliver locally while supporting increasingly global and sophisticated investment needs.

Client expectations are also evolving. A new generation of affluent customers expects seamless, personalized experiences that bring together banking, lending, investments and payments within a single relationship. Rather than viewing wealth management as a standalone business, leading institutions are integrating wealth propositions across the broader banking journey, using data and AI to provide more proactive advice, tailored investment strategies and deeper client engagement.

Technology is accelerating this transformation. AI-powered relationship management, intelligent portfolio insights, digital onboarding and automation are improving both advisor productivity and client experience, while emerging capabilities such as tokenized assets and digital custody are beginning to expand the range of investment opportunities available to sophisticated investors. Yet technology alone will not differentiate market leaders. Success will depend on combining digital innovation with trusted advisors, integrated client data and operating models that deliver personalized experiences at scale.

Looking ahead, wealth management in the Middle East will increasingly become a strategic growth engine rather than a specialist banking service. As competition intensifies, institutions that can build connected wealth ecosystems, bringing together advisory, investments, payments and lending into a seamless client experience will be best positioned to strengthen client loyalty, unlock new sources of fee income and capture the region's next phase of wealth creation.

How Capco can help

Turning emerging trends into competitive advantage requires more than technology adoption. It demands the right strategy, operating model and execution capabilities. Capco partners with financial institutions across the Middle East to help translate innovation into scalable business outcomes.

In cross-border payments, Capco supports banks in modernizing payment ecosystems, optimizing liquidity strategies and preparing for the next generation of settlement infrastructure as the industry moves toward smarter, more transparent payment models.

For organizations exploring Agentic AI, Capco helps identify high-value use cases, strengthen governance frameworks and scale adoption in a controlled and measurable way. Through Capco Smart Suite and its broader AI capabilities, firms can accelerate value realization while maintaining appropriate oversight and control.

In sovereign cloud, Capco supports clients in designing resilient cloud strategies, evaluating hyperscaler and partner ecosystems, strengthening governance and controls, and building the foundations required to scale both cloud and AI adoption with confidence.

Capco helps financial institutions define their digital asset strategy, assess opportunities across the tokenization value chain and develop the operating models, governance frameworks and technology capabilities required to support institutional adoption of tokenized assets.

In wealth management, Capco helps banks navigate the evolving wealth landscape by aligning operating models, digital capabilities and client engagement strategies with changing customer expectations.

Model charges are only a fraction of the true cost of enterprise AI. The real cost is what it takes to turn AI outputs into a business outcome that delivers value, meets control requirements and can be repeated at scale.
          

      

The economics of enterprise AI has moved beyond the procurement question. Rather than ‘what does a token cost’, the better question is: what does it cost to produce an accepted business outcome with AI – and how can that cost be governed and optimized as adoption scales?

An organization can negotiate a lower model rate and still make AI-enabled work more expensive. The supplier’s invoice records tokens, seats and other metered services, but it does not capture the platform infrastructure, human review, exception handling and rework required to deliver the desired result. To reach a successful outcome, specific thresholds and standards must be met around completion, quality, risk, control and timeliness.

Consider an AI-enabled mortgage servicing workflow. Model usage fees may be modest, yet that workflow can still be ‘costly’ if the system retrieves irrelevant documents, requires repeated interactions to establish the necessary context or escalates items unnecessarily for human review. If the output then fails a required quality or control check, the workflow has consumed resources without producing an acceptable outcome.

Simply put, your AI bill is not your AI cost. The bill records supplier-facing meters. The cost accrues across the complete workflow. An accepted outcome is completed work that meets the agreed business, quality and control requirements.

The invoice captures meters, not the work

The management remit is already broadening. In the FinOps Foundation's 2025 survey, 63% of 861 respondents (representing some $69 billion in public-cloud spend) said their practices managed AI spending, up from 31% a year earlier.¹ This reflects a broader shift: AI economics can no longer be managed solely through model pricing. 

Microsoft makes the same point in its Foundry guidance, noting that model and platform charges need to be considered alongside the infrastructure and services required to run the application.²

For management purposes, the complete cost boundary has four components: 

    

execution cost, including attempts, retries, retrieval, tools, compute and fallbacks

    

allocated shared platform cost, including gateways, orchestration, observability, evaluation infrastructure, storage and licenses

    

required human work, including review, supervision, correction and exception handling

    

attributable failure cost, such as remediation or incident response.

Controls add cost, but they are not waste

Validation, audit evidence, access controls and human approval can all increase direct expense, but they also reduce the likelihood or consequences of failure. Removing them simply to improve a cost metric creates a false economy. The pertinent question is whether an individual control is necessary and proportionate in the context of a desired outcome.

Leaders should not assume their model invoice is where the biggest cost saving opportunity sits. In some workflows, human review, shared platforms or failure and rework will dominate; in others, they will not. Measure the workflow first, then focus management attention where the evidence points.

Architecture determines the economics of execution

The most capable model is not necessarily the right model for every task. At enterprise scale, architecture can route simpler work to lower cost models, escalate only when additional capability is required, and control context, reasoning, retries and agentic loops. Using higher-performing technology when a simpler solution delivers the required outcome simply creates unnecessary cost.

The objective is not simply to minimize token consumption but to use the lowest cost architecture capable of consistently delivering the required outcome. This makes cost optimization an engineering discipline and reduces reliance on every user making the most cost-efficient choice every time.

Behavior changes the economics

How individuals use AI can materially change workflow economics. Poorly scoped requests, unnecessary context, repeated iterations and choosing AI when another tool would suffice all lead to avoidable consumption. More context, more iterations and more powerful models consume additional resources, and those effects compound at scale. Sustainable economics therefore requires both disciplined user practices and platforms that make the efficient choice the easy choice.

Scaling AI also scales costs

AI proofs of concept may result in relatively small bills, but those figures are not a yardstick for what the same workflow will cost when used by thousands of people or embedded in core processes. The question is not simply the cost of AI investment today, but how AI economics behave at enterprise scale.

This is particularly important for agentic AI, where a single business request can trigger planning, retrieval, tool calls, validation, retries and multiple model interactions. One user interaction can translate into many underlying units of consumption. At scale, small inefficiencies in workflow design can compound rapidly.

For financial services leaders, tracking AI spend is therefore only the starting point. The challenge is to forecast it, govern it and engineer it for sustainable scale while preserving the required business and control outcomes. Successful adoption does not automatically translate into sustainable economics.

Cost per accepted outcome

The useful unit of measurement is therefore not a model response, but an accepted business outcome.

Complete cost per accepted outcome = complete attributable workflow cost / unique outcomes that pass every agreed gate

This changes how competing solutions should be compared. A cheaper model is not cheaper if it creates more retries, human review or exceptions. Equally, a more expensive model may reduce the total cost of completing the work. Compare the full cost of reaching the same accepted outcome, not the price of an individual model call.

Token-level measures still matter, but primarily as diagnostic data. Engineers still need model-level data (including input and output tokens, repeated context and reasoning) to understand where cost is being generated. Different audiences need different measures. 

Engineers need model and system telemetry to identify inefficiency. Workflow owners need to understand review, rework and exceptions. Executives need to know the total cost of producing the business outcome. The principle is simple: use technical measures to diagnose the cost but manage the economics at the level of the business outcome.

Five actions for your next planning cycle

Define one accepted outcome. Choose a material workflow and agree the eligible case, completion event, quality and control gates, timeliness requirement and maturity window.

Set the complete cost boundary. Include execution, allocated platform, required human work, and attributable failure. Assign each cost once and tag necessary control cost separately.

Create a traceable join. Connect invoice records and model telemetry to stable workflow, case, attempt, and outcome identifiers. Treat missing attribution as a data-quality problem.

Compare equivalent workflows. Hold the workload and acceptance rubric constant while testing changes to context, routing, tools, caching, validation, or loop controls.

Scale on outcome evidence. Approve wider deployment when complete cost improves without weakening agreed quality, risk, control, timeliness, or maturity guardrails.

Conclusion

Invoices from AI providers remain an essential source of financial truth. They become useful in decision making only when connected to the work, people, controls and failures involved in producing an accepted outcome.  AI economics should therefore be managed at the level of the business outcome, with architecture, controls and operating practices used to manage the cost of getting there.

The AI bill can be measured. AI economics have to be engineered.

References

1 https://data.finops.org/2025-report/

2 https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/concepts/manage-costs

title: Finanza e rischio cyber: non basta prepararsi, bisogna dimostrarlo

fullText:
Nel 2026 i servizi finanziari dovranno affrontare minacce informatiche sempre più evolute, dalla crescita dell’IA agentica al rischio quantistico. Regolatori, DORA, NIS2, zero trust, fornitori ICT e convergenza tra frodi e cybercrime spingono verso controlli più misurabili e operativi.

      

Dall’ascesa delle minacce legate all’intelligenza artificiale agentica e autonoma alla sfida imminente del calcolo quantistico: una serie di minacce emergenti sta mettendo in luce nuove vulnerabilità nei servizi finanziari.

Con un atteggiamento intransigente delle autorità di regolamentazione di fronte a risposte lente e a una sicurezza informatica insufficiente e con le tradizionali difese ritenute non più adeguate, la domanda non è più “come vi state preparando?”, ma “dimostrateci che siete pronti”.

Nel contesto europeo e italiano, questo cambio di paradigma è ulteriormente accelerato da normative come DORA e NIS2, che richiedono evidenze concrete di resilienza operativa.

Sicurezza informatica nei servizi finanziari 2026: le priorità

Il percorso corretto prevede un potenziamento dei controlli, adottando difese avanzate basate sull’IA per aumentare la resilienza, una gestione solida del rischio legato ai complessi ecosistemi dei fornitori e l’integrazione della sicurezza in ogni area dell’azienda.

Mentre le minacce continuano a evolversi, cinque tendenze chiave plasmeranno l’agenda della sicurezza informatica per il 2026.

Conformità: il passaggio a un’applicazione più attiva

Storicamente, gli organismi di regolamentazione hanno spesso cercato di stare al passo con il settore in termini di emanazione e applicazione di linee guida e normative relative alla tecnologia. Tuttavia, l’urgenza relativa ai controlli di sicurezza si è evoluta negli ultimi anni e, fino al 2026, si prevede che le autorità di regolamentazione continueranno a orientarsi verso un’applicazione più rapida e attiva. Le istituzioni saranno tenute a dimostrare progressi tangibili e sostenibilità – attraverso l’integrazione di solidi processi di sicurezza nei propri modelli operativi – anziché limitarsi a strategie o piani.

Non è più sufficiente dimostrare che i controlli esistono. I loro effetti devono essere misurabili e i controlli devono essere in grado di rispondere alle minacce in continua evoluzione. Questa analisi è particolarmente importante per quanto riguarda le tecnologie emergenti. Per esempio, le autorità di regolamentazione stanno ora integrando la governance dell’IA direttamente nei requisiti di gestione del rischio. Questo è coerente con l’AI Act europeo, che introduce obblighi specifici per i sistemi di intelligenza artificiale ad alto rischio.

Inoltre, cresce la pressione per dimostrare di essere pronti ad affrontare le minacce future, come quelle che emergeranno a seguito dell’avvento dell’informatica quantistica.

Le linee guida del NIST per l’informatica post-quantistica prevedono la creazione di un inventario delle risorse crittografiche, quali chiavi e certificati, una chiara comprensione delle lacune e delle vulnerabilità, nonché la disponibilità a dimostrare i progressi compiuti nell’implementazione delle nuove raccomandazioni e di tecnologie volte alla risoluzione dei problemi.

Per il 2026, il messaggio ai vertici aziendali è chiaro. La conformità non è più una semplice verifica di aver compiuto gli interventi necessari, ma una dimostrazione continua dell’efficacia del controllo operativo.

IA contro IA: la velocità della difesa

Nel 2026, l’intelligenza artificiale ridefinirà le regole della sicurezza informatica. L’IA agisce come un moltiplicatore di attacchi, amplificando vettori di minaccia che in precedenza erano difficili da eseguire e abbassando la barriera di ingresso per gli attori malevoli. Ciò include una proliferazione di “IA generativa avversaria”, compresi i deep fake e sofisticate tattiche di impersonificazione che aggirano i metodi di verifica tradizionali.

L’unico modo per contrastare queste minacce basate sull’IA è implementare difese basate sull’IA. Gli analisti umani, per quanto competenti, non riescono più a tenere il passo con il volume e la velocità degli attacchi automatizzati. Gli istituti finanziari devono potenziare i propri team con capacità di rilevamento e risposta automatizzati.

Tuttavia, questa transizione comporta dei rischi. Per implementare l’IA in modo sicuro all’interno dell’ecosistema di un’organizzazione saranno necessari nuovi controlli e misure di sicurezza. Le aziende devono colmare il divario di competenze all’interno dei propri team e attuare un’adeguata gestione del cambiamento per favorire l’adozione dell’IA.

La priorità per quest’anno è quella di adeguare i team operativi affinché possano lavorare in modo efficace a fianco degli agenti di IA, in un ambiente regolato da politiche rigorose che definiscano esattamente cosa questi potenti strumenti possano e non possano fare.

Zero trust: l’identità come nuovo perimetro

Il perimetro di rete tradizionale è ormai superato. Al suo posto, lo zero trust si è evoluto da semplice termine di moda a requisito imprescindibile del settore. Non più una semplice implementazione tecnologica: lo zero trust è oggi una mentalità fondamentale in cui un’organizzazione non si fida mai implicitamente di nulla o di nessuno.

Un elemento chiave di questa architettura è l’“identità”, che ora rappresenta il perimetro di fatto per le imprese moderne. Prevediamo che il 2026 vedrà una spinta continua verso robuste autenticazioni multifattoriali (MFA) e gestione degli accessi basata sull’identità (IAM), con particolare enfasi nel panorama italiano, dove molte organizzazioni stanno ancora affrontando la complessità di integrare questi modelli con infrastrutture legacy e sistemi IAM frammentati. Ancora una volta, le autorità di regolamentazione pongono domande mirate, passando da «Qual è la vostra strategia Zero Trust?» a «Perché non è stata implementata completamente?»

I rischi si estendono dai dipendenti fino ai clienti. Stiamo assistendo alla necessità di controlli più rigorosi sull’identità dei clienti – come l’autenticazione adattiva abilitata dall’analisi comportamentale e dall’intelligenza dei dispositivi – per aiutare a proteggere i clienti dalle frodi e dalle violazioni degli account. Gli istituti finanziari devono trattare ogni richiesta di accesso, che provenga da un dipendente, da un bot o da un cliente, con la stessa rigorosa attenzione.

Rischio di ecosistema: catena di fornitura e adeguamento alle sfide future

La definizione di “organizzazione” si è ampliata. Nel 2026, i fornitori terzi fanno di fatto parte dell’ecosistema interno di un istituto – e i loro rischi sono i rischi dell’istituto stesso. Anche un sistema di sicurezza interna di livello mondiale può essere violato da un fornitore che utilizza software obsoleto. Nel contesto italiano, caratterizzato da filiere articolate e da una forte presenza di fornitori di piccole e medie dimensioni, questo rischio è particolarmente rilevante.

L’affidamento ai principali fornitori di servizi cloud implica che un fallimento di un singolo soggetto terzo potrebbe avere un impatto sistemico su più istituzioni finanziarie. Le autorità di regolamentazione considerano il fallimento di un fornitore come un fallimento della banca stessa, richiedendo alle istituzioni di applicare ai propri fornitori gli stessi rigorosi controlli che applicano alla propria infrastruttura. DORA rafforza ulteriormente questo aspetto, richiedendo una gestione strutturata dei fornitori ICT critici e una piena visibilità sui rischi associati.

Convergenza tra criminalità informatica e criminalità finanziaria

All’inizio del 2026, la convergenza tra sicurezza informatica e criminalità finanziaria continua a evolversi. Grazie all’introduzione di tecniche basate sull’intelligenza artificiale, stanno emergendo nuove tattiche su entrambi i fronti.

Le organizzazioni stanno ora comprendendo il valore dell’integrazione dei dati provenienti dai sistemi SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) e da altri strumenti di registrazione e monitoraggio con i dati provenienti dai controlli antifrode e antiriciclaggio (AML). Questa integrazione consente una potente analisi comportamentale in grado di “collegare i puntini” tra i modelli di comportamento degli utenti e gli eventi di criminalità finanziaria, rendendoli vulnerabili alle minacce informatiche (un rischio che è aumentato significativamente con la guerra in Iran) man mano che diventano più interconnessi.

Conclusione: pronti per il futuro

Con l’intensificarsi delle minacce e l’attività delle autorità di regolamentazione, nel 2026 è l’operatività, piuttosto che l’intenzione, a determinare la leadership nel campo della sicurezza informatica.

La visione di Capco per il 2026 è quella di una sicurezza adattiva, integrata e sostenibile per un mondo in cui la sicurezza non ha un perimetro statico, ma è un ecosistema intelligente e basato sui dati.

Nonostante il panorama possa apparire scoraggiante, con tecnologie in rapida evoluzione esposte a un numero crescente di minacce, ci sono motivi per rimanere ottimisti. La consapevolezza dell’evoluzione delle minacce informatiche non è mai stata così elevata e gli strumenti a disposizione dei difensori non sono mai stati così efficaci.

Questo articolo è stato originariamente pubblicato su Agenda Digitale.
